prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology and active form of glucagon-like peptide-1 that established the basis for incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: The round-1 exchange did not weaken the scientific case for B005; it narrowed the dispute to one name and one question about what the citation should claim. All six of us describe a mature chain: proglucagon processing, the incretin effect and human physiology, identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide, receptor and tissue biology, and then agonists with independently replicated outcome-trial benefit in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. Nobody argues for waiting. I keep Holst, Drucker and Mojsov because that trio is the one that can be credited as discovery: native physiology and the active peptide (Holst), the active form and its synthesis (Mojsov), and receptor, tissue and translational biology (Drucker). The one change from round 1 is to the citation, not to the names. I now narrow it to the physiology and active form of GLP-1 and to the basis it gave for treatment, and I no longer let it read as if it credited the therapies themselves. That answers Sandberg's stated condition for accepting a Mojsov trio, and it is more honest about whom the prize names.
statement.case_against: The weakness I cannot remove is credit. A three-person cap cannot hold both Mojsov and Knudsen, Habener sits outside the credited names, and Mojsov's weight relative to Habener and to Holst's earlier work cannot be settled from the file. Several of us, myself included, are working partly from recollection of the history, and agreement among six people who know the same well-told story is not verification. If the committee decides the clinical transformation cannot be separated from acylated analogue design, my trio honours the hormone but not the molecules that reached patients, and a Drucker, Holst and Knudsen configuration would be the more coherent prize. I regard that as a legitimate position and not an error, but I have not been persuaded that Knudsen's work is an original discovery on the same footing as the identification of the active peptide.

responses.point: Linnarsson prefers Drucker, Holst and Knudsen so that one citation spans physiology and the development of long-acting therapy, and says B006 is the cleaner configuration if the committee will not credit drug development or cannot settle the Mojsov question.
responses.response: I have reread your argument and I agree that Knudsen's acylation-based design was decisive for dosing interval and for the drugs that produced outcome-trial evidence. Where I still differ is on what the prize is crediting. The identification of the active peptide is upstream of every analogue, and a prize that includes drug design while leaving the discoverer of the active form unnamed inverts that order. I also do not think the unresolved Mojsov-Habener question is a reason to move to B006. It is a reason to be exact in the citation, which I have now done. On your fallback, B006 stays my first alternative, but I would use it only if the committee found that no B005 trio could be defended, and I do not think that point has been reached.

responses.point: Sandberg says she could move to a Mojsov trio if the citation were narrowed to physiology and peptide identification, and otherwise prefers Knudsen because the therapeutic half of the citation would be left without a named contributor.
responses.response: Your condition is fair and I have met it. My citation now names the physiology and active form of GLP-1 and says only that these established the basis for incretin-based treatment. It does not claim the development of the therapies. I accept your point that this leaves Knudsen unnamed and that the cost is real, but a citation scoped to what the three laureates actually did avoids the problem you describe, since it makes no claim about long-acting drugs that would need a named contributor. On B021, I agree with you that the Eshhar gap is more serious than the cap on B005, because it cannot be solved by choosing among the credited names. That is the reason I hold B021 as my second alternative and not my first.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would accept the Linnarsson trio if Mojsov's priority proved too uncertain, and her summary of my round-1 file mentions caution about Sabatini (B047) because of documented conduct concerns.
responses.response: On the first point, I agree this is a close call and not a firm split, and I think the narrowed citation is what lets the Mojsov trio hold. I need to correct the record on Sabatini. My round-1 statement did not raise a conduct question and I have no verified facts on it. I do not want it to enter attribution, and I would set it aside unless a member puts documented facts before the committee. The chair's questions already noted it is not in the file. My reasons for not preferring B047 are scientific: Hall's priority on TOR, the three-name credit and the lack of first-place support. I agree with you that debate is best spent on candidates with cleaner attribution.

responses.point: El Manira would not block a Knudsen variant, says dropping Mojsov on grounds of the cap would resolve a disputed credit by omission, and treats imatinib (B050) as the strongest drug-development case if the committee wanted one.
responses.response: I agree that removing a name only because of the cap is not an argument, which is why I rest on what each person did and not on the cap alone. Your point on B050 is useful for a different reason: it shows the committee can honour development when the foundational discoveries are also credited, and that condition is not met for B005 with Knudsen, nor for B050 where the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL fusion work sit outside the names. I take your readiness to accept a Knudsen variant as a sign that the real difference between us is small, and I would rather hold the discovery citation clearly than split the difference.

responses.point: Perlmann places B006 second as a clean, textbook mechanism with a secure Walter and Mori credit, says it is a sound candidate for a later year or a second part, and would not penalise it for lacking a drug.
responses.response: I agree with you on the science and on not penalising B006 for lacking a drug. On the chair's question about a two-part prize, I have tested it and I would not accept it this year. B005 plus B006 would leave one name for GLP-1 under the three-person cap, and removing either Holst or Drucker to make room is a loss of credit that I cannot defend on the evidence. My shared work with you on dopamine neurons does not bear on this judgement. B006 therefore remains a strong candidate for the next cycle, and my first alternative if B005 fails.

uncertainties: Mojsov's weight relative to Habener and others, which cannot be resolved from the file, and how much of my own account of the GLP-1 history rests on memory and not on documents.
Whether a committee that prefers to honour drug design would find a discovery-scoped citation too narrow, and whether a Knudsen trio would then be the better single configuration.
Whether B006 or B021 is the better fallback if B005 attribution cannot be defended, since B006 has clean credit but indirect medical link, and B021 has stronger clinical record but the Eshhar gap.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted credited name. As chair I disclose about twenty co-authored works with committee member Thomas Perlmann (dopamine neurons, Nurr1, autophagy; count not audited) and a postdoctoral period with Paul Greengard, who is not a candidate. Neither involves a shortlisted candidate, and I infer no further ties. I have no verified information on any conduct question concerning B047 and treat it as outside the record. No change from round 1 and no recusal requested.
